study.title: Missing-value strategies and indicators
study.locator: 8.4.2 univariate median and most_frequent strategies; 8.4.6 Marking imputed values: MissingIndicator, or add_indicator=True on the imputer, to keep a missingness flag beside the imputed value; 8.4.7 which estimators accept NaN directly

focus: Fit every statistic on training rows only, then transform the rest. Refitting on evaluation rows leaks their distribution into the features.
OneHotEncoder with handle_unknown=ignore writes a new category as all zeros; with handle_unknown=error it raises. Pick one before serving.
StandardScaler centers, so it densifies sparse input unless with_mean=False. MaxAbsScaler preserves sparsity.
A missingness indicator keeps the fact of missingness after imputation fills the value. Dropping the flag assumes missingness carries no signal.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, build a two-column pipeline on five training rows: median-impute and standardize a numeric column, one-hot encode a categorical column with handle_unknown=ignore. Transform two new rows, one with an unseen category and one with a missing number, and write the exact output rows including the all-zeros encoding.
traps: Fitting the imputer or scaler on the full data before splitting. Validation scores then reuse evaluation statistics.
Setting sparse_output=False on a high-cardinality encoder inside a pipeline. Memory grows with rows times categories; keep sparse until an estimator needs dense.
Reading the percentile-flattened income as deleting outliers. It remaps tails to fixed bins; the IsolationForest drop in the same notebook is a separate commented-out choice.

selfTest.q: A scaler fit on all 10,000 rows gives mean 5.2; fit on the 8,000 training rows gives 5.0. Which one goes into the pipeline, and why?
selfTest.a: The training-only 5.0. The full-data mean carries evaluation rows into every transformed training value.

selfTest.q: OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown=ignore) trained on [a, b] sees [c]. What row does it emit, and what does inverse_transform return for it?
selfTest.a: It emits [0, 0]. inverse_transform maps all zeros back to None when no category was dropped. Verified with scikit-learn 1.9.

selfTest.q: Why does StandardScaler on a CSR matrix raise unless with_mean=False?
selfTest.a: Centering subtracts the mean from every entry including stored zeros, which would densify the matrix. With with_mean=False only scaling applies and sparsity survives.

selfTest.q: When does an imputed column need a companion indicator column?
selfTest.a: When missingness itself predicts the target, for example sensors that fail under load. The indicator keeps that signal after the value is filled.

study.depth: Treat the 0.005 threshold as a starting point, not an optimum: the notebook reports no gain there. Skip Exercises 1, 2 and 4 here.

focus: Selection inside the pipeline is fit on training folds only. Selecting on all rows before cross-validation picks features with evaluation help.
ColumnTransformer drops unlisted columns by default under remainder=drop. Name every kept column or set remainder explicitly.
ClusterSimilarity and ratio features are fit state too: their centers and medians come from training rows and must serialize with the pipeline.
joblib saves the fitted object, not the build script. Reload in a fresh process and compare predictions before trusting the artifact.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, sketch a ColumnTransformer with a median-plus-scaler numeric path and a most-frequent-plus-one-hot categorical path, state the remainder behavior, and write the three-line joblib save, load and predict-parity check.
traps: Calling fit_transform on the test set with the same pipeline object. It refits every statistic on evaluation data; call transform only.
Tuning the SelectFromModel threshold on the test score. The notebook run at 0.005 shows no gain; tune it under cross-validation or hold it fixed.
Saving the model but rebuilding preprocessing by hand in serving. Any median, category list or cluster center that differs silently shifts every prediction.

selfTest.q: Where does SelectFromModel sit relative to the cross-validation split, and what breaks if it sits outside?
selfTest.a: Inside, fit on training folds only. Outside, the selector sees evaluation labels and the error estimate turns optimistic.

selfTest.q: A new column appears in serving data. What does ColumnTransformer do with it?
selfTest.a: It ignores it. The column list, including the remainder, is fixed at fit, so the new column is dropped even under remainder=passthrough. That is silent, so add a schema test that fails on unexpected columns.

selfTest.q: A joblib reload matches old predictions, but new-category rows differ from training time. Is the artifact broken?
selfTest.a: Not necessarily. handle_unknown=ignore maps new categories to all zeros by design. The parity check is identical predictions on fixed rows plus the declared unknown policy.

Choose the component count from cumulative explained variance and reconstruction cost, and write tests invariant to sign.
units.why: PCA is the baseline representation for wide tabular data and the preprocessing step inside the clustering and anomaly cards. Its signs are arbitrary, so any test that hard-codes them is wrong.

next.note: Cluster in PCA space and compare stability with and without reduction.

study.title: PCA lab with scaling and sign
study.locator: Principal Components Analysis on USArrests: scaling before PCA, scores via transform, the biplot with its y-axis reflection note, standard deviations and PVE with the scree plot

focus: PCA centers but does not scale. Features in larger units dominate the first components; standardize first when units differ.
Component variance is s_j squared over n-1; the ratio divides by the total. Randomized solvers approximate both.
Component signs are arbitrary: flipping a component with its scores leaves every reconstruction unchanged. Tests must use absolute values or reconstruction error.
The cumsum rule at 0.95 is a budget, not an optimum. Downstream error and cost decide the count.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, center [[1,2],[3,4],[5,6]], run the SVD, and report first component [0.7071, 0.7071], singular value 4 and explained ratio 1.0. Then state the sign-flip invariant and the reconstruction from one component.
traps: Hard-coding component signs from one run. Sign conventions differ across libraries, solvers and versions; assert with abs or compare reconstructions.
Calling PCA(n_components=0.95) a fixed dimension. It selects whatever count reaches 95 percent on the fitted data; refitting on new data can change the width.
Using randomized-solver inverse_transform as exact. The docs note it is not the exact inverse of transform even with whiten=False.

selfTest.q: Why do [[1,2],[3,4],[5,6]] yield ratio 1.0 on one component?
selfTest.a: Centered rows are multiples of [1,1], so the matrix has rank one. The single singular value 4 carries all variance. Verified with NumPy: s=[4,0].

selfTest.q: Two runs give components [0.7,0.7] and [-0.7,-0.7] with mirrored scores. Which one is wrong?
selfTest.a: Neither. A joint sign flip of a component with its scores preserves projections and reconstructions; only mixed or unmirrored comparisons fail.

selfTest.q: Two features have variances 1 and 10000. What happens without scaling, and what changes with it?
selfTest.a: Without scaling the first component follows the large-variance feature almost entirely. Standardizing puts both on equal footing; do it when units are arbitrary.

selfTest.q: Randomized PCA reports slightly different ratios on each seed. Is that a bug?
selfTest.a: No, it is an approximation. Fix the seed for reproducibility and use the exact solver when exact ratios matter.

Implement Lloyd iterations from a blank file with k-means++ seeding and a fixed iteration cap.
Diagnose empty clusters, seed instability and k choice with inertia, silhouette and repeated runs.
units.why: k-means is the first clustering mechanism and the initializer inside Gaussian mixtures. Its objective only descends, never to a global promise, so seeds and k decide the answer.

next.note: Contrast partition geometry with density and merge geometry.

study.title: k-means on simulated data
study.locator: K-Means Clustering: K=2 separation on the simulated 50-point data with random_state, K=3 splitting behavior, and inertia_ as within-cluster sum of squares
study.depth: The lab says the n_init default is 10; that predates scikit-learn 1.4. The default is now auto, one run under k-means++, which is why the lab passes n_init=20 explicitly.

focus: Each assignment step and each mean update cannot increase the inertia, so Lloyd iterations converge, usually to a local minimum. Restarts pick among minima.
Since version 1.4 the default n_init=auto runs once under k-means++ and ten times under random init. One k-means++ run is not ten restarts.
Inertia always falls as k grows. Read k from elbows, silhouette and repeated-seed stability, never from one inertia value.
Empty clusters happen when a center loses every point. Know the repair: re-seed, drop, or error.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, run one Lloyd round on [[0,0],[0,1],[5,0],[5,1]] from centers [[0,0],[5,1]]: labels [0,0,1,1], new centers [[0,0.5],[5,0.5]], inertia 2.0 down to 1.0. State why the next round cannot raise it.
traps: Comparing inertia across different k or seeds as quality. Inertia is comparable only for fixed data, fixed k and best-of-restarts.
Assuming n_init=10 always. Under the default k-means++ the auto default is a single run; set n_init=10 explicitly when stability matters.
Requesting more clusters than samples. scikit-learn 1.9 raises an error for n_samples=3 with n_clusters=5; it does not return empty clusters silently.

selfTest.q: Why do Lloyd iterations terminate?
selfTest.a: Assignments are finite and the inertia never increases: neither the assignment step nor the mean update can raise the objective, so the loop ends at a fixed assignment or max_iter.

selfTest.q: Two seeds give inertia 120 and 95 at k=5. Which clustering wins on the objective, and what stays unknown?
selfTest.a: The 95 run wins on inertia. Whether either is near the global optimum or the right k stays unknown; check silhouette and seed spread.

selfTest.q: A center gets no points in one iteration. Name two sound repairs.
selfTest.a: Re-seed it at a far point such as the highest-inertia contributor, or drop it and continue with k-1. Either way record the event.

selfTest.q: Silhouette prefers k=2 on two stretched blobs while the task needs subgroups. What do you do?
selfTest.a: Keep the task k and justify it downstream. Silhouette rewards convex separation; it does not know the use.

units.title: Gaussian mixtures and EM
outcomes: Explain responsibilities as posterior component membership and the EM loop as alternating E and M steps.
Derive the 1D M-step updates for means, variances and weights from weighted maximum likelihood.
Select the component count with BIC or AIC and state why a plain GaussianMixture always uses every component.
units.why: Mixtures turn distance into probability: overlapping groups get graded membership plus density scores that the anomaly unit spends.

next.note: Spend mixture densities as anomaly scores with a declared threshold.
Compare soft parametric groups with density and merge structure.

study.locator: Gaussian Mixtures: EM-fitted weights, means and covariances on the three-ellipsoid data with the covariance_type full, tied, spherical and diag comparison; Selecting the Number of Clusters with the BIC and AIC formulas and the minimum at k=3
study.depth: Skim Bayesian Gaussian Mixture Models; variational inference is later work. Keep the BIC and AIC minimum plot.

study.title: EM estimation, init and failure modes
study.locator: 2.1.1 Gaussian Mixture: EM E-step and M-step description, covariance options, the singularity and always-uses-all-components cons, and the BIC asymptotic note; Choice of the Initialization method with the k-means default

focus: Responsibilities are posteriors that sum to one per point. The M-step refits each Gaussian to responsibility-weighted data.
Likelihood rises every EM round but only to a local optimum. Starts matter; the sklearn default starts from k-means.
Full covariance needs d(d+1)/2 parameters per component. Few points per component invite singular covariances; reg_covar (1e-6 by default) adds to the diagonal to keep them invertible.
BIC penalizes parameters with log(m) times p. It recovers the true count only asymptotically under a true mixture; on real data it is a guide, not proof.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, write the 1D E-step responsibility formula and the M-step updates for mean, variance with MLE denominator, and weight. Run the K=1 case on [2,4,6]: mean 4.0 and variance 8/3=2.6667.
traps: Dividing the M-step variance by n-1. Mixture MLE divides by the responsibility sum, which is n for K=1, giving 2.6667 on [2,4,6], not 4.0.
Reading converged likelihood as a global optimum. Different starts converge differently; report spread, not one run.
Trusting the BIC minimum as truth on misspecified data. The docs note asymptotic recovery needs data truly drawn from a mixture.

selfTest.q: What does responsibility 0.9 of point x under component 2 mean?
selfTest.a: Posterior membership: under current parameters the probability is 0.9 that component 2 generated x. It is not a hard label.

selfTest.q: K=1 EM on [2,4,6] gives variance 2.6667. Derive it.
selfTest.a: Mean 4.0; squared deviations 4+0+4=8; MLE divides by 3. The unbiased 4.0 answers a different question.

selfTest.q: Weights converge to [0.99, 0.01] on two overlapping groups. What do you conclude?
selfTest.a: One component explains nearly everything. Try K=1, check BIC, and consider that the small component fits outliers.

selfTest.q: Full covariance on 50 points in 10 dimensions with K=5. What breaks?
selfTest.a: Each full covariance needs 55 parameters from about 10 effective points. Expect singularities; use tied or diag, regularize, or cut K.

units.why: Real groups are rarely spheres. Density and merge views find moons and hierarchies that k-means smears, but their knobs decide the answer.

study.locator: DBSCAN: make_moons(1000, noise=0.05) at eps=0.05 (7 clusters, many points labeled -1) versus eps=0.2 (two clusters, no noise), core_sample_indices_, components_, and KNN on the cores with a 0.2 distance cutoff to label new points; Other Clustering Algorithms: AgglomerativeClustering with complete linkage on [0,2,5,8.5]
study.depth: Skim the Spectral Clustering bonus code; keep the eps contrast and the linkage example.

study.title: Density, linkage and metric limits
study.locator: 2.3.7 DBSCAN: dense definition from eps and min_samples, core, border and outlier rules, the eps-must-be-tuned warning with all-noise and merged-cluster failures; 2.3.6 hierarchical clustering: Ward, complete, average and single linkage with the uneven-size guidance; 2.3.11 metrics: silhouette formula with its convex-cluster bias and the adjusted Rand index correcting for chance

focus: eps sets the neighborhood radius and min_samples the density floor. On the notebook moons, eps=0.05 breaks the two moons into 7 clusters and labels 7.7 percent as noise, while 0.2 finds the two moons with no noise; always sweep eps.
Linkage defines merge distance: single follows chains, complete compacts, Ward prefers equal-variance merges. On [0,2,5,8.5] single splits off 8.5 while complete pairs neighbors.
DBSCAN labels new points only by extra machinery: the notebook trains KNN on cores. The clusterer itself has no predict.
Silhouette rewards dense convex separation and can punish correct density shapes. Pair it with stability and downstream checks.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, hand-run DBSCAN with eps=2.0 and min_samples=2 on [[1,1],[1.5,1.5],[2,1],[8,8],[8.5,8.5],[9,8]]: two core groups [0,0,0,1,1,1] with no noise. Then move one point to [100,100] and show it becomes -1.
traps: Leaving eps at 0.5 on unscaled features. eps lives in feature units; scale first or the radius is meaningless.
Calling -1 a detected anomaly set. It means not dense enough under this eps; nearby eps values relabel it.
Reporting silhouette alone on moons. On the notebook moons a k-means split scores 0.49 and the true moon labels 0.33; the docs warn that silhouette favors convex clusters.

selfTest.q: On the notebook moons, eps=0.05 gives 7 clusters and 7.7 percent noise, while eps=0.2 gives two clean moons. What went wrong at 0.05, and what does the -1 label mean?
selfTest.a: The radius is too small for the sampling density. A core needs min_samples points within eps, counting itself, so sparse stretches of each moon lose their cores and the moons fragment. A -1 point is within eps of no core: not dense enough under these settings, which is not the same as anomalous.

selfTest.q: Single linkage gives [0,0,0,1] and complete gives [1,1,0,0] on [0,2,5,8.5]. Which is right?
selfTest.a: Both follow their definitions: single chains through small gaps, complete caps the largest within-cluster distance. The task decides which grouping is useful.

selfTest.q: On the notebook moons, KMeans(2) scores silhouette 0.49 and the true moon labels score 0.33. Which clustering is better?
selfTest.a: The true moons. Silhouette rewards compact convex groups, so it ranks the wrong spherical split higher. Use stability, adjusted Rand against any known structure, and downstream checks.

selfTest.q: Two DBSCAN runs with close eps values disagree on 5 percent of labels. What do you report?
selfTest.a: The disagreement rate and which points flip, usually borders. Stability is evidence; one label vector is not.

study.title: Novelty versus outlier contract and detectors
study.locator: 2.7 Novelty and Outlier Detection: outlier versus novelty definitions, contamination, offset_, decision_function sign and predict labels; 2.7.2 novelty prediction on new data; 2.7.3 EllipticEnvelope robust covariance, IsolationForest path lengths and LOF local density with its fit_predict-only default; 2.7.4 novelty detection with LOF (novelty=True)

focus: Outlier methods fit on polluted data; novelty methods fit on clean data and judge new points. LOF with novelty=False has no predict for new data; refit with novelty=True.
contamination sets the score cutoff as a percentile through offset_. It declares the alert rate; it does not discover it.

IsolationForest isolates with random feature splits; anomalies need fewer splits. In the paper's score, near 1 means anomaly, well below 0.5 means normal, and all scores near 0.5 mean no distinct anomaly; scikit-learn's score_samples returns the negative. Trees stop at depth ceil(log2(n)) for n samples per tree.
Rescale or re-encode and the ranking changes: LOF neighborhoods, elliptic envelopes and GMM densities all live in the given coordinates.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, fit IsolationForest with contamination=0.25 and random_state=42 on [[0],[0.1],[0.2],[10.0]]: predict gives [1,1,1,-1] with only the last decision_function negative. State the implied alert rate and why the cutoff is a policy.
traps: Tuning contamination until the known incident appears, then reporting the hit as detection. The threshold was fit to the answer; hold it fixed or cross-check on other windows.

Calling LOF fit_predict on a deployment batch. With novelty=False the batch is judged against itself, not against clean history, and predict does not exist. Fit on clean data with novelty=True, then call predict on new points.
Comparing raw score_samples across models or scalings. Scores are model-and-coordinate specific; compare ranks or calibrated alert rates.

selfTest.q: Training data is clean and the task judges next week points. Outlier or novelty setup?
selfTest.a: Novelty: fit on clean history and predict new points. An outlier setup would fit the polluted batch including the points under test.

selfTest.q: contamination=0.25 on 100 training points. How many train alerts, and what does offset_ do?
selfTest.a: About 25: offset_ is the score percentile implementing that rate. It does not estimate the true anomaly fraction.

selfTest.q: Standardizing a skewed sensor channel shuffles LOF rankings. Is that a bug?
selfTest.a: No. LOF compares local densities in the given units; rescaling rewrites every neighborhood. Record scaling as part of the detector.

selfTest.q: A GMM 2 percent rule flags a new batch at 9 percent. What do you report?
selfTest.a: The flag rate rose from 2 to 9 percent, 4.5 times, under a fixed threshold. Report the shift with counts and slices before touching the threshold.

practice.note: The tests check rounded score vectors on a 5-point set with one outlier at random_state=42 and a tight cluster at random_state=123. They match only the learn section's recipe taken literally: np.random.seed, legacy np.random calls, and c(n) = 2(ln(n-1) + 0.5772156649) - 2(n-1)/n for every leaf size above 1, so c(2) is about 0.154. The paper and scikit-learn set c(2) = 1, which fails these vectors; note that difference rather than treating it as a bug.

outcomes: Explain what t-SNE preserves in local neighborhoods and what it distorts in global distances, densities and cluster sizes.
Run t-SNE and UMAP with fixed seeds, scaled input and recorded perplexity, n_neighbors and min_dist.
Refuse semantic claims from embedding shapes without stability and downstream checks.
units.why: Embeddings are maps for the eyes, not measurements. Unlabeled shapes become false findings unless every knob is recorded and every shape is re-tested.

focus: t-SNE minimizes KL between neighborhood probabilities; the objective is non-convex, so seeds differ. Record the seed and try more than one.
Perplexity sets the effective neighbor count; n_neighbors trades local detail for global shape; min_dist packs or spreads the plot. None of them is a cluster count.
sklearn TSNE has no transform for new points; UMAP has transform. Refitting t-SNE on each new batch rebuilds the map.
Sizes, gaps and densities on the plot are layout artifacts until stability runs and labels say otherwise.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, list the guarded recipe: scale, fix the seed, record perplexity or n_neighbors with min_dist, run two seeds, and state two invalid readings: cluster size as population and gap width as distance.
traps: Clustering the 2D embedding and reporting the groups as found structure. The map distorts distances; validate in the original space.
Reading big gaps as big separations. min_dist and perplexity set the spread; change them and gaps move.
Fitting t-SNE once and shipping the picture. One seed is one local minimum; rerun and keep only stable shapes.

selfTest.q: Two t-SNE seeds show different island counts on the same data. Which map is right?
selfTest.a: Neither yet. Rerun several seeds, keep shapes that persist, and check them with labels or clustering in the original space.

selfTest.q: Why scale before t-SNE or UMAP?
selfTest.a: Both use neighbor distances. An unscaled large-unit feature decides every neighborhood; StandardScaler puts features on shared footing.

selfTest.q: UMAP transform embeds new digits but sklearn TSNE cannot. Why?
selfTest.a: UMAP keeps the fitted model and its transform places new points into the existing embedding. scikit-learn's TSNE has fit_transform but no transform, so new points need a refit that rebuilds the whole map.

selfTest.q: A UMAP plot shows one class as three islands. Claim: three subtypes. Allowed?
selfTest.a: As a hypothesis only. Islands can come from n_neighbors, min_dist and seed choices; test with stability runs and independent evidence.
